back: The ease with which workers can move between occupations (occupational) or between places (geographical) to work.
The ease with which workers can change from one type of job to another.
The ease with which workers can move from one area to another to take up work.
Specific skills, cost and length of training, qualifications and licensing, lack of education, age, discrimination.
Housing costs, family and social ties, moving costs, lack of information, culture or language, immigration rules.
Retraining grants and apprenticeships (occupational); housing, transport, job information and relocation help (geographical).
Unemployment in declining areas or industries alongside labour shortages in growing ones (structural unemployment).
The emigration of skilled workers: the home country loses skills it paid to train, though it may gain remittances.

front: Consequences of changes in mobility for firms
back: Higher mobility makes vacancies easier and cheaper to fill; lower mobility causes skill shortages and higher wage costs.
